prize_parts.citation: for the development of aberration-corrected electron microscopy, enabling imaging and spectroscopy of matter at sub-angstrom resolution

statement.case_for: Aberration correction broke the limit that Scherzer's 1936 theorem seemed to impose, and it did so by an original, verifiable experiment: the hexapole corrector built and demonstrated in the TEM in 1997-1998 and then shown to deliver sub-angstrom resolution. The result is not a refinement of an existing capability. It opened a door, because individual atoms, interfaces, dopants and defects can now be imaged and analysed spectroscopically in routine work across physics, materials science and chemistry. Maturity is not in question: more than two decades of independent confirmation, instruments in laboratories worldwide, and a decisive role in quantum-material, catalyst and device research. Attribution is the cleanest on the list. Rose supplied the corrector theory and design, Haider led the construction of the first working corrector, and Urban drove the experimental realization and demonstrated what it could resolve, which gives three people who did the original work.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that the supplied credit leaves out the parallel STEM-corrector line (Krivanek and collaborators), so three names may not capture the full historical record, and I do not want to be the member who waves that away. A second objection is that this is an instrument invention and some colleagues will say the discovery content is thinner than for a new phenomenon. My own field proximity is a risk to my judgement here, and I am the only member who put this first. The case should be tested by colleagues who do not work with electron microscopes every day. If the committee finds that a fair prize cannot be built from these three names alone, I would not insist on it.

responses.point: Pearce ranked aberration-corrected TEM fourth with a clean and fair three-person attribution, but wondered whether chemistry or another committee is the more natural home for microscopy, as with the 1986 prize.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution is clean, and I appreciate the support. On the home question I would point out that the 1986 microscopy prize to Ruska, Binnig and Rohrer was a physics prize, so the electron microscope as a physics invention has precedent in this committee. The physics content is also real. Controlling the electron optics at that level is a physics achievement, and the resulting atomic-scale spectroscopy of interfaces, oxygen vacancies and electronic structure is condensed-matter physics. I accept that the user base is broader than physics.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B039 seventh and B051 first. He sees the corrector invention as well established and timely but with a weaker discovery element, and notes that Krivanek and Dellby's STEM correction lies outside the credited names.
responses.response: The Krivanek point is the serious qualification and I share it. My reading of the record is that the TEM corrector (Rose, Haider, Urban) and the STEM corrector are distinct inventions and the first working demonstration of sub-angstrom resolution by correction came from the TEM line, so I think Rose, Haider and Urban fit a prize for TEM correction. But I want that checked by the expert reports before we commit, and I accept that the citation must be worded precisely. On the weak discovery element I disagree in part. The Nobel statutes say invention, and the invention here removed a limit once thought fundamental. I do agree that B051 is a strong alternative, and I rank it second.

responses.point: Kroll put optical lattice clocks first because Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's record accuracy extended time and frequency metrology by orders of magnitude, and credit between them is clean.
responses.response: I accept the scientific case for the lattice clock and put it high as an alternative. My reservation is about who did the original work. Katori made the proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations, so his claim is the original one. Ye's decisive contribution is taking the clock to record accuracy and stability, which is the 'did it much better' step that I think the committee should weigh carefully against the original discovery. The prize cannot reward the best result in place of the first. I am also not yet persuaded that it is sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I would want the expert reports on priority between Katori, Ye and the SYRTE group before I move my vote.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked IceCube first as a genuine discovery found in nature that opened a new window, and accepts that credit within a large collaboration is difficult but workable with three names.
responses.response: I ranked IceCube fifth because I agree with the scientific case. It is an experimentally verified new window with a diffuse flux seen in 2013. My concern is the one you raise yourself: with a collaboration of this size I am not 'absolutely sure' the three credited names are those who did the original work, and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage complicates it. Source identification is also still thin, so a few more years would strengthen the case. I would not oppose it, but I do not think it is ahead of the aberration-corrected microscope on attribution.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked topological insulators first, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the most defensible split of theory plus first experiment, and acknowledged that it leaves out Hasan and other early credit.
responses.response: This is a major field and I ranked it fourth. My difficulty is the same one you identify. Allocation among Kane, Mele, the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Molenkamp's experiment and Hasan's ARPES observations is not settled, and the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs on the timing. I included Hasan in place of Mele because the 3D observation is an original experiment in its own right, but I concede that this is a choice between defensible options and not a clear reading of the record. I do not think the topological insulator case is ahead on attribution either.

uncertainties: Whether a fair prize for aberration-corrected electron microscopy can be formed from the three supplied names without the STEM-corrector line (Krivanek, Dellby).
Whether the committee will treat an instrument invention as a physics prize in this year, given that only I ranked it first.
For optical lattice clocks, who made the original contribution between Katori and Ye, and whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited.
For magic-angle graphene, how to treat the lead experimental authors (Cao, Fatemi) and the earlier moire graphene experiments outside the three credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No personal tie to Rose, Urban, Haider or the credited names on other ballots is apparent from my profile. I am an electron microscopist and head a Chalmers microscopy group, so field proximity to B039 is a real bias that colleagues should discount, and I have worked with Tokyo, Kyushu and Tohoku microscopy communities. I will defer to the chair on whether recusal on B039 is warranted. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague but works in circuit QED, which is not my preferred ballot.
